**Summary (1–2 lines):** A large, bi-temporal, multi-sensor (optical+SAR) dataset and 9-task benchmark for disaster assessment across 36 events; 14 VLMs are evaluated, and 4 are fine-tuned, showing consistent gains and cross-sensor robustness.

**Strengths**

* Well-motivated scope (disaster response), realistic task taxonomy spanning perception→reasoning→reporting.  
* Inclusion of SAR and pre/post imagery is distinctive and practically important.  
* Careful construction and QC; broad evaluation yielding useful insights (SAR gap, counting sensitivity).  
* Fine-tuned baselines improve reliably; code/data available; author commitment to ongoing updates.

**Weaknesses (now largely addressed)**

* Initial clarity issues (abbreviations, task setup), reliance on LLM-as-judge for open-ended tasks, potential geographic skew, MCQ choice for counting; metadata gaps (Croissant/RAI fields).

**Rebuttal & discussion:** Authors added human evaluation and multi-evaluator checks (consistent rankings), US vs non-US performance analysis, structured open-ended counting with RMSE, clarified abbreviations (DSR/BBR), expanded model coverage (incl. LLaVA-NeXT, GPT-4.1-mini) and scaling results for PSALM, and pledged better documentation (damage-level guidelines) and updates. All reviewers are positive; two at **5**, the third indicated an upward revision after rebuttal.

**Decision & rationale:** **Accept.** The dataset is original, substantial, and sound; it fills a clear gap (multi-hazard, multi-sensor, multi-task) and provides strong baselines and analysis. Ethical risks are minimal, and documentation is improving. High expected impact for remote sensing and multimodal evaluation.

**Presentation recommendation:** **Spotlight.** Broad community interest, clear novelty (SAR+bi-temporal \+ end-to-end disaster workflow), and strong empirical evidence.

**Notes to authors (actionable):**

* Report inter-annotator agreement for damage labels; include representative edge-case examples.  
* Finalize Croissant/license and populate RAI fields; fix any broken resource links.  
* Document privacy choices (e.g., de-geocoding) explicitly.  
* Add discussion/experiments on multi-resolution and SAR polarimetry as future extensions.  
* Release scripts for human-eval and structured counting evaluation.

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

Thank you very much for your prompt response and constructive suggestion!

> **R2:** While lines 194–202 provide a list of abbreviations, I notice that LUC and BBD are not included.

Thank you very much for bringing this to our attention and for your careful reading of the manuscript. You are right that 'LUC' and 'BBD' were not included in the abbreviation list. To clarify, 'LUC' refers to our disaster scene recognition task (which should be consistently abbreviated as 'DSR'), while 'BBD' refers to bearing-bodies recognition (which should be 'BBR'). We will ensure all instances are corrected to use 'DSR' and 'BBR' consistently throughout the manuscript and properly include all abbreviations in the revision. We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's attention and meticulous review.



> **R6:** I understand that MCQs are generally preferred for evaluation. However, my concern was specifically about the disaster type and counting tasks. For counting, in particular, it should be feasible to instruct the model to provide answers in a specific format, as is commonly done in math reasoning benchmarks, to facilitate extraction and evaluation.

Thank you for this insightful question regarding the counting task evaluation. We appreciate your thoughtful suggestion about alternative evaluation approaches for these specific tasks. To clarify our current approach, existing benchmarks' counting tasks in the general domain \[1] and remote sensing \[2]\[3] predominantly utilize multiple-choice formats, and we initially followed these established practices. However, we acknowledge your point that using structured output formatting is well-taken. Open-ended evaluation can indeed help VLMs provide more natural responses while avoiding the potential issue of randomly selecting correct answers in MCQ format.



Following general practices in structured evaluation for large language models \[4], we prompted *\<answer>number\</answer>* formatting to capture responses, allowing VLMs to retain their reasoning process while providing answers in a standardized, extractable format.  We assessed VLM performance using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) as the evaluation metric for Building Damage Counting (BDC) and Damage Road Estimation (DRE) tasks.  RMSE quantifies the deviation between predicted values and ground truth annotations, and lower RMSE values indicate better counting accuracies. The comparative results between open-ended (RMSE) and multiple-choice questions (OA) are as follows:


| 　                         | ↓RMSE  |       | ↑OA   (%) |      |
| ------------------------- | ------ | ----- | --------- | ---- |
| Method                    | BDC    | DRE   | BDC       | DRE  |
| LLaVA-OV                  | 114.32 | 10.37 | 26.4      | 24.2 |
| InternVL3-8B              | 86.93  | 10.17 | 30.3      | 24.1 |
| InternVL3-14B             | 102.03 | 12.11 | 27.4      | 23.6 |
| InternVL3-78B             | 105.96 | 9.53  | 29.4      | 28.7 |
| Qwen2.5-VL-3B             | 95.04  | 17.86 | 29.9      | 21.2 |
| Qwen2.5-VL-7B             | 69.66  | 4.27  | 34.2      | 29.3 |
| Qwen2.5-VL-32B            | 76.61  | 3.91  | 33.2      | 30.9 |
| Qwen2.5-VL-72B            | 53.83  | 7.83  | 34.8      | 28.9 |
| GPT-4o                    | 127.51 | 14.86 | 24.2      | 21.4 |
| GPT-4.1                   | 115.89 | 9.6   | 25.5      | 25   |
| Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Fine-tune) | 61.39  | 4.73  | 34.3      | 29.4 |
| InternVL3-8B (Fine-tune)  | 108.88 | 10.18 | 29.1      | 24.9 |

**The comparative performance demonstrates that models maintain consistent relative rankings across both evaluation formats, validating the robustness of our MCQ design.** For disaster type recognition, we conducted experiments but found evaluation challenges when models generate specific event names (e.g., "Mount Vesuvius eruption" instead of "volcano"), making automated assessment difficult. Providing predefined categories in prompts yielded results similar to our MCQ approach, suggesting that the structured format effectively captures the underlying capabilities. We will incorporate these additional evaluation strategies in our revised manuscript to provide researchers with flexible assessment options.

Thank you again for your suggestions! We hope our response can address your concerns, and please let us know if you have any further questions.

*[1] Chen, L., et al. (2024). Are we on the right way for evaluating large vision-language models?. NeurIPS 2024.*

*[2] Danish, M. S., et al. (2024). Geobench-vlm: Benchmarking vision-language models for geospatial tasks. ICCV 2025.*

*[3] Wang, F., et al (2025). Xlrs-bench: Could your multimodal llms understand extremely large ultra-high-resolution remote sensing imagery?. CVPR 2025.*

*[4] Tam, Z. R., et al. (2024). Let me speak freely? a study on the impact of format restrictions on performance of large language models. EMNLP 2024*.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for recognizing DisasterM3 as the first comprehensive vision-language benchmark for disaster response and management, appreciating our practical 9-task taxonomy, good dataset quality control, multi-sensor approach, and extensive experimental analysis. Here, we carefully address your concerns in detail:

>**Q1:** Considering that this is a dataset work, the author should evaluate the model more extensively. For example, evaluate more commercial models; more series, such as the LLaVA series, which, due to its completely open source nature, makes it easier for downstream people to study what data combinations can work in disaster scenarios.

Additionally, we could explore knowledge distillation as an implicit regularization strategy. Self-distillation [4] from the original pre-trained weights could help preserve generalizability during fine-tuning for counting tasks.

The previous use of "GPT4" was indeed imprecise as it referred to the model family rather than specific versions. Our ground-truth anchored approach significantly mitigates self-preference bias because: (1) evaluation focuses on alignment with expert-defined criteria rather than subjective preferences, (2) scoring is based on factual accuracy and completeness relative to established standards, and (3) the presence of reference answers provides objective benchmarks that constrain evaluator subjectivity.

**R6:** Thank you for this insightful question regarding our task formatting choices. We adopted the multiple-choice question (MCQ) format to ensure standardized and reproducible evaluation across our diverse disaster tasks, following the widely accepted practice in the VLM community.

The MCQ format is recognized as the standard approach for evaluating VLM knowledge capabilities because different models exhibit varying instruction-following abilities, and open-ended formats present significant evaluation challenges due to response ambiguity and inconsistent formatting. This explains why numerous established benchmarks, including generic datasets (MMStar [1], SEED-Bench [2], MMMU [3]), medical benchmarks (GMAI-MMBench [4]), and remote sensing evaluations (XLRS-Bench [5]), consistently adopt MCQ formats for rigorous evaluation. summary.value: This paper introduces DisasterM3, a new large-scale, remote sensing vision-language dataset specifically designed for disaster damage assessment and response. The primary contributions are threefold: 1) The dataset itself, which is characterized by its multi-hazard (10 disaster types), multi-sensor (paired optical and SAR images), and multi-task (9 hierarchical tasks from recognition to report generation) nature. 2) A comprehensive benchmark of 14 existing VLMs, which reveals their limitations in complex disaster scenarios, particularly in understanding SAR imagery and performing fine-grained counting. 3) A set of strong baselines established by fine-tuning four representative VLMs on DisasterM3, demonstrating significant performance improvements and the dataset's effectiveness for domain adaptation.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The dataset's design directly addresses a critical real-world problem. The inclusion of paired optical and SAR imagery is a standout feature that tackles the all-weather, all-time monitoring challenge often hindered by clouds and rain during disasters. This multi-sensor aspect is novel and sets it apart from existing remote sensing VLM datasets (e.g., TeoChatlas, EarthVQA), which primarily focus on optical imagery and more general geospatial tasks. The authors clearly justify this distinction in the introduction and related work sections.

2. The 9-task taxonomy (Figure 1) is exceptionally well-conceived. It moves beyond simple VQA or captioning to create a pipeline that mirrors a real disaster response workflow: from initial scene recognition, to quantitative damage assessment (counting buildings/roads), to precise localization of key objects, and finally to generating high-level, actionable reports. This multi-task structure provides a much richer and more challenging benchmark than prior work.

3. The construction pipeline (Figure 6), which combines LLM-aided generation with human expert annotation and multi-round verification, ensures high data quality. With 26,988 bi-temporal images and 123k instruction pairs across 36 real disaster events, the dataset is substantial enough to support robust model training and evaluation.

4. The paper provides an extensive evaluation of 14 diverse VLMs, including open-source, commercial, and domain-specific models. The analysis is insightful, going beyond just reporting scores. For instance, the paper uncovers key findings such as the "domain gap" for disaster scenarios (Table 2), the severe performance degradation on SAR data (Figure 7), and the performance variation across different disaster types (Table 4) and object densities (Figure 8). These findings are valuable for the community to understand the current capabilities and limitations of VLMs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
While the work is very strong, there are a few minor limitations and areas for potential improvement:

1. The paper annotates building damage into 'intact', 'damaged', and 'destroyed' following FEMA guidelines. However, in practice, the distinction between 'damaged' and 'destroyed' can be subjective, especially from aerial imagery. A brief discussion in the appendix about the inter-annotator agreement or the challenges faced during this labeling process would strengthen the credibility of the damage-related tasks (e.g., DBC in Table 2).

2. The analysis in Section 4.2 and Figure 8 honestly points out that the fine-tuned InternVL3-8B model shows signs of overfitting on the building counting task (performance degrades in some density ranges after fine-tuning). While the authors acknowledge this, the paper could benefit from a more proactive discussion on potential mitigation strategies. For example, suggesting techniques like data augmentation, regularization methods, or exploring more sophisticated numerical reasoning modules could provide a more complete picture for future work.

3. The paper states all optical and SAR images were resampled to 0.8m resolution. This standardization is necessary for a controlled experiment. However, in real-world applications, disaster response teams work with data from a wide variety of sensors with different resolutions. A limitation of the current work is that it does not evaluate how models trained on DisasterM3 would generalize to imagery of different spatial resolutions. This could be mentioned as a direction for future research.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

The rebuttal solved all of my concerns. I keep the rating unchanged (to 5).

Thanks all authors, AC, and PC.

summary.value:
The paper introduces DisasterM3, a vision-language dataset specifically curated to support research in remote sensing for disaster damage assessment and response. The dataset is designed to encompass multiple disaster events across different geographic regions. Notably, DisasterM3 incorporates both optical and SAR images, addressing real-world challenges where optical sensors may fail, thereby providing a realistic benchmark for model robustness across sensor modalities. The tasks included are diverse and align closely with real disaster scenarios, spanning recognition, counting, segmentation, relational reasoning, and the generation of comprehensive disaster reports.

In addition to the dataset, the authors present extensive benchmarking results using a broad selection of state-of-the-art vision-language models. The evaluations highlight the limitations of current general-purpose and specialized models in handling complex disaster scenes, particularly emphasizing issues such as the inability to generalize across different disaster types and sensor modalities, as well as insensitivity in tasks that require precise counting and detailed reasoning. The paper further explores fine-tuning several open-source models on the DisasterM3 dataset, demonstrating significant improvements across all tasks.

strengths_contributions.value:
* Significance:
The DisasterM3 dataset provides a comprehensive vision-language benchmark designed for disaster response scenarios. Its large-scale and diverse scope enables the development and evaluation of multimodal models for real-world disaster situations, significantly enhancing their practical utility and potential societal impact (Section 1).

* Novelty:
DisasterM3 stands out by incorporating both optical and SAR imagery, as well as bi-temporal image pairs (pre- and post-disaster), allowing detailed analysis and reasoning tasks across a range of disaster scenarios. This careful curation addresses key shortcomings found in prior datasets, including limited disaster types, reliance on single sensors, and restricted task complexity, providing a uniquely comprehensive platform for multimodal model development and assessment (Section 3).

* Benchmarking:
The authors rigorously benchmark 14 state-of-the-art vision-language models, clearly identifying the current capabilities and limitations of these models. Their thorough analysis highlights critical performance gaps, including insufficient disaster-specific knowledge, difficulties in accurately counting damaged objects, and limited segmentation precision, providing valuable insights and strong baselines for future research (Section 4).

* Methodological Contributions:
Through domain-specific fine-tuning of established vision-language models on DisasterM3, the authors achieve significant performance improvements across diverse tasks. This methodological advancement highlights the effectiveness and necessity of targeted fine-tuning for enhancing the robustness and accuracy of multimodal models in disaster-related applications (Section 4).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
* Lack of Discussion on Dataset Limitations: The paper does not sufficiently address the limitations of the dataset or tasks, either in the main text or the Appendix. Aside from briefly mentioning overfitting during fine-tuning on one specific task, there is little substantive discussion regarding possible weaknesses of the dataset, such as annotation biases, representativeness, or coverage.   
Suggestion: Include a dedicated section in the main paper discussing the limitations of the dataset and benchmarks, addressing potential annotation issues, geographic or event-type biases, and any coverage gaps.

* Presentation and Clarity Issues: Certain columns in Table 2 (e.g., LUC, BBD) are not introduced or defined in the main text, and their meaning is only clarified in the Appendix. Additionally, the process for obtaining ground truth for the referring segmentation task is not explained in detail. There is also ambiguity in Section 3.2 regarding the use of the GPT-4o, GPT4-o, and GPT4 models: it is unclear whether these refer to the same or different models, particularly in the context of report polishing (GPT4).

* LLM-based Evaluation Concerns: The evaluation metrics for disaster captions and restoration advice rely exclusively on GPT-based scoring (Section 4, Table 2). Given recent findings that LLMs often exhibit self-preference bias [1], there is a risk that models from the GPT-4 family may be favored in evaluation, potentially skewing results and diminishing the reliability of comparative model assessment.  
Suggestion: Supplement LLM-based automatic evaluations with a human assessment on a representative subset of the data and analyze the correlation between GPT4.1 scoring and human judgments to validate the robustness and fairness of the evaluation.

* Potential Geographic Bias: While the dataset includes events from various global regions, nearly half of the disaster events originate from the United States (Figure 2). This could result in models that generalize poorly to other geographic regions, undermining the dataset's claimed global applicability.  
Suggestion: Perform an analysis of model performance on US-based versus non-US-based disaster events, both before and after fine-tuning, to assess and quantify any regional disparities. 

* Practical Utility and Task Formatting: Several tasks, including disaster type recognition (DTR) and counting, are presented in multiple-choice question (MCQ) format (Section 3.2). However, for both practical and evaluation purposes, some of these tasks could have been framed as open-ended questions, which better reflect real-world disaster response scenarios and more effectively assess model reasoning capabilities. The rationale for using the MCQ format in these cases is not sufficiently explained.  
Suggestion: Experiment with and report results for open-ended QA formats for DTR and counting tasks, and discuss the trade-offs between MCQ and open-ended approaches from both practical and evaluative perspectives.

Reference:
 [1] Panickssery, Arjun, Samuel Bowman, and Shi Feng. "LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (2024): 68772-68802.

It would be valuable to analyze whether model performance on these shared tasks within DisasterM3 correlates with performance on established general benchmarks. Such an analysis could clarify whether DisasterM3 presents unique challenges or reflects broader trends in multimodal model capabilities.

summary.value: This paper introduces DisasterM3, a comprehensive remote sensing vision-language dataset specifically designed for disaster damage assessment and response applications. The authors address a critical gap in existing vision-language models for the domain-specific applications by creating a specialized dataset that handles the unique challenges of disaster scenarios, including extreme weather conditions, diverse geographic regions, and multiple sensor modalities (Optical Images & SAR). The dataset encompasses 26,988 bi-temporal satellite images and 123,010 instruction pairs covering 36 historical disaster events across five continents. The work establishes a systematic benchmark for evaluating VLMs on disaster-related tasks and demonstrates that fine-tuning on disaster-specific data significantly improves model performance in emergency response scenarios.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Important Dataset, DisasterM3: The authors created the world's first vision-language benchmark targeting disaster management and response, DisasterM3. It is much bigger than the current derivative dataset, such as TEOChat's disaster part, containing 36 disaster events across 10 disaster types, across five continents, which is large-scale and comprehensive. The dataset is built upon xBD, BRIGHT, and the Maxar Open Data Program, constituting the largest open-source disaster dataset currently available. On this foundation, establishing VLM data represents a novel approach with significant contributions to the field. The benchmark provided can very well fill the gap in this field, enabling researchers and developers to investigate the application value of VLMs in this important remote sensing application. Furthermore, the pixel-level road analysis capability can make substantial contributions to the entire disaster response and management domain.

2. Novel Task Taxonomy: DisasterM3 has 9 essential disaster-related tasks progressing from basic recognition to complex reasoning. These tasks are meaningful for the practical use of VLMs for disaster management and response.

3. Good Quality Control: The quality control framework described in the article is reasonable and impressive. I downloaded the data and checked some of it, and it indeed possesses high quality.

4. Multi-Sensor Integration: DisasterM3 incorporated both optical and SAR imagery to address the challenge of optical sensor limitations during extreme weather conditions in disaster scenarios, filling the gap in disaster-related VLM datasets.

5. Validation of Effectiveness: The authors utilized extensive experiments to demonstrate that their proposed instruct data can enhance VLMs' perception in disaster scenarios.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Considering that this is a dataset work, the author should evaluate the model more extensively. For example, evaluate more commercial models; more series, such as the LLaVA series, which, due to its completely open source nature, makes it easier for downstream people to study what data combinations can work in disaster scenarios.

title.value: DisasterM3: A Remote Sensing Vision-Language Dataset for Disaster Damage Assessment and Response

abstract.value: Large vision-language models (VLMs) have made great achievements in Earth vision. However, complex disaster scenes with diverse disaster types, geographic regions, and satellite sensors have posed new challenges for VLM applications. To fill this gap, we curate the first remote sensing vision-language dataset (DisasterM3)  for global-scale disaster assessment and response. DisasterM3 includes 26,988 bi-temporal satellite images and 123k instruction pairs across 5 continents, with three characteristics: **1) Multi-hazard**: DisasterM3 involves 36 historical disaster events with significant impacts, which are categorized into 10 common natural and man-made disasters. **2) Multi-sensor**: Extreme weather during disasters often hinders optical sensor imaging, making it necessary to combine Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery for post-disaster scenes. **3) Multi-task**: Based on real-world scenarios, DisasterM3 includes 9 disaster-related visual perception and reasoning tasks, harnessing the full potential of VLM's reasoning ability with progressing from disaster-bearing body recognition to structural damage assessment and object relational reasoning, culminating in the generation of long-form disaster reports. We extensively evaluated 14 generic and remote sensing VLMs on our benchmark, revealing that state-of-the-art models struggle with the disaster tasks, largely due to the lack of a disaster-specific corpus, cross-sensor gap, and damage object counting insensitivity. Focusing on these issues, we fine-tune four VLMs using our dataset and achieve stable improvements (up to 10.4\%$\uparrow$QA, 2.1$\uparrow$Report, 40.8\%$\uparrow$Referring Seg.) with robust cross-sensor and cross-disaster generalization capabilities. Project: https://github.com/Junjue-Wang/DisasterM3.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
